title: Hand-Span Measuring
subject: math
learningGoal: Measure length with repeated equal units and see why units must be the same size.
realWorldHook: Long ago people measured with hands and feet. Today we use rulers so everyone gets the same answer.

materials.item: A table or bed to measure
materials.householdSubstitution: Any long object: a sofa, a door, a rug

noPurchaseRoute: Nothing needed except hands and a long object at home.
parentPreview: You and your child each measure the same table in hand spans, get different numbers, and figure out why. It introduces the idea that units need to be equal.

parent.parentSays: How long is our table? Let's measure it with our hands.

child.screen: How long is the table? Let's measure with hands!
child.readAloudText: How long is the table? Let's measure with our hands.

parent.parentSays: Spread your hand wide and walk it along the edge without gaps. Count the spans.
parent.whyThisWorks: Units laid end to end without gaps or overlaps is the core idea behind every ruler.

child.screen: Measure the table with your hand. How many hands long?
child.readAloudText: Spread your hand. Walk it along the table. Count.

parent.parentSays: Now I'll measure with my hand. Count my spans with me.

child.screen: Count your grown-up's hand spans. How many?
child.readAloudText: Now count your grown-up's hand spans.

parent.parentSays: Why did we get different numbers if the table didn't change?
parent.whyThisWorks: Discovering that the unit size matters is why we need standard units.

child.screen: Why did you get different numbers?
child.readAloudText: Why did you get different numbers?

parent.parentSays: Ask the two check questions below. Give your child time to think, then note how each one went.
What could we use so we always get the same answer?

expectedResponses: Child's number is bigger because their hand is smaller
We need a unit that is always the same size

misconceptions.signal: Leaves gaps or overlaps hands while measuring.
misconceptions.supportiveNextQuestion: Let's make sure each hand starts exactly where the last one ended.

misconceptions.signal: Thinks the table is longer when measured by the child because the number is bigger.
misconceptions.supportiveNextQuestion: Did the table grow? Or was the hand smaller?

checkQuestions.parentAsks: If a giant measured our table with their hand, would they get a bigger or smaller number?

interpretation.clear: Says smaller, because the giant's hand is bigger.
interpretation.partial: Says smaller but can't say why.

child.screen: A giant measures the table with a giant hand. Bigger or smaller number?
child.readAloudText: A giant measures the table with a giant hand. Bigger or smaller number?

checkQuestions.parentAsks: How could two friends in different houses compare their beds fairly?

interpretation.clear: Suggests using the same object (a ruler, the same string, the same book).
interpretation.partial: Suggests measuring but not with a shared unit.

child.screen: How can two friends compare beds in different houses?
child.readAloudText: How can two friends compare their beds fairly? Tell your grown-up.

extension: Measure with spoons, then with a book. Which unit gives the biggest number? Why?
accessibilityAdaptations: Use a toy car or shoe as the unit if hand spans are hard.
